Definition: Collective right of colonized peoples to reclaim sovereignty over their political, cultural, and economic lives. A fundamentally transformative process that requires the dismantling of colonial institutions, the decolonization of consciousness, and the creation of new social and political forms rooted in the experiences of the formerly colonized.

Recovery and exercise of Indigenous political authority grounded in land, law, and relational ontologies that predate and exceed the state's jurisdiction. State-recognized self-government arrangements typically reproduce colonial power relations rather than displacing them.

Alternative epistemology of law and repair, rooted in non-Western and Indigenous legal traditions, that prioritizes the restoration of relationships, community healing, and accountability over punitive retribution.

Vision of a world in which multiple ontologies, knowledges, and ways of organizing social and political life coexist on equal terms rather than one in which a single Western-liberal model of peace is imposed as universal. It requires the active decolonization of peace discourse and practice.

A type of peace conceived from the perspective of those who have been historically silenced by colonial modernity. It fundamentally challenges the colonial matrix of power that has produced and sustained violence in the first place. It is inseparable from the broader decolonial project of epistemic delinking from Western frameworks.

Inherent, collectively held political authority of Indigenous peoples over their lands, governance, and cultural reproduction; an authority that derives from Indigenous legal and relational traditions rather than from recognition or delegation by the settler-colonial state.
